title: Responsible AI & Ethics
subtitle: Bias, Fairness, Safety, and Accountability
content:
⚖️ Why Responsible AI Matters

AI systems are deployed in high-stakes domains - hiring, lending, healthcare, criminal justice, education. Errors and biases at scale cause real harm. Building capable AI without building responsible AI is a reputational, legal, and ethical liability.

This is not optional. Regulations like the EU AI Act, NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and sector-specific laws increasingly require documented, auditable AI practices.

🎯 Bias and Fairness

Where bias enters: Training data (historical bias, sampling bias), label bias, model bias, deployment bias.

Fairness definitions (no single "fair" - they conflict):

  • Demographic parity: Outcomes independent of protected attribute
  • Equal opportunity: Equal true-positive rates across groups
  • Equalized odds: Equal true-positive and false-positive rates

Mitigation: Audit datasets for representation; reweight samples; use fairness constraints; test on slices, not just averages.

🛡️ Safety and Alignment

Alignment = ensuring model behavior matches human intent and values.

  • Hallucinations: LLMs confidently produce false statements. Verify outputs; never trust without checking.
  • Prompt injection: Untrusted text can override instructions. Treat all external input as untrusted.
  • Jailbreaks: Attempts to bypass safety training. Layered defenses, never a single control.
  • Goal misgeneralization: Models pursue proxy goals that look right in training but wrong in deployment.

📊 Evaluation Beyond Accuracy

Accuracy alone is misleading. Evaluate on:

  • Slice performance: Per-group metrics, not just averages
  • Robustness: Distribution shift, adversarial inputs
  • Calibration: Are confidence scores trustworthy?
  • Human eval: For LLMs, use human raters and rubrics
  • Toxicity / harm: Automated + manual review

🔐 Privacy and Data

  • PII: Don't train on personal data without a lawful basis.
  • Memorization: LLMs can regurgitate training data. Use differential privacy or scrub-and-audit.
  • Data provenance: Document where data came from and what consent was given.

📋 Accountability and Transparency

  • Model cards: Document intended use, performance, limitations.
  • Datasheets: Document dataset collection, composition, uses.
  • Human-in-the-loop: For high-stakes decisions, keep a human accountable.
  • Right to explanation: Provide reasons for automated decisions where required.

✅ Practical Checklist

  • Define intended use and out-of-scope uses explicitly
  • Audit training data for representation and consent
  • Measure performance on slices, not just the aggregate
  • Test for hallucination, prompt injection, and jailbreaks before launch
  • Publish a model card; maintain an incident response plan
  • Monitor in production; have a kill switch

questions.question: A model has 95% overall accuracy but 60% accuracy for one demographic group. What is the right conclusion?

options.text: The model is biased and needs investigation - aggregate accuracy hides slice-level failures
95% is high enough to deploy
Bias only matters if the model is intentional
Add more data of any kind and the problem will resolve

questions.explanation: Aggregate metrics can mask serious per-group failures. Always evaluate on slices; high overall accuracy is not a substitute for fairness analysis.

questions.question: An LLM confidently states a fake citation. What is this called and what should you do?

options.text: Hallucination - verify outputs before relying on them
A bug - report it and the model will be retrained
Prompt injection - ignore it
Overfitting - reduce the learning rate

questions.explanation: LLMs can hallucinate plausible but false content. Always verify factual claims, especially citations and numbers, before using them.

questions.question: A retrieved document tries to override your system instructions, instructing the model to ignore prior rules. What is this and how do you defend?

options.text: Prompt injection; treat retrieved content as untrusted input, keep system instructions privileged, and validate outputs against a schema
A hallucination; lower the temperature
Overfitting; train more
A normal feature; nothing needs to be done

questions.explanation: Prompt injection is untrusted text trying to override instructions. Defense: treat retrieved/document content as data, mark it as untrusted, reinforce privileged instructions, and validate outputs.

questions.question: Two fairness criteria conflict - you can't satisfy demographic parity and equal opportunity at the same time. What's the right move?

options.text: Document the trade-off explicitly and pick the criterion appropriate for the use case; fairness is plural, not single-criterion
Always pick demographic parity; it's the only definition that matters
Always pick equal opportunity; it's the only definition that matters
Ignore fairness criteria entirely

questions.explanation: Multiple fairness criteria are known to be mutually unsatisfiable in many settings. Choosing one is a values decision the team must make explicitly and document.

questions.question: Which is the best doc + accountability practice when shipping an ML model?

options.text: Publish a model card (intended use, performance, limitations) and a human-in-the-loop plan for high-stakes decisions
Ship it; docs are optional
Only ship after accuracy reaches exactly 100% (unrealistic)
Skip docs and rely on internal notes

questions.explanation: Model cards and human-in-the-loop plans make intended use, limitations, and accountability explicit - increasingly required by regulation and good AI hygiene generally.
